title: Reactor

validation.research: Seven primary sources: Schmidt’s original Reactor paper (including Dispatcher/Notifier aliases), the original Proactor paper, official Python selectors and Socket Programming HOWTO documentation, libuv design documentation, Linux epoll manual, and Project Reactor introduction. The pattern is readiness dispatch rather than asynchronous operation completion or the JVM reactive-streams library. Waiting, registration, callback dispatch, per-connection framing, partial reads/writes, would-block, EOF, resource ownership, loop thread confinement, offloaded blocking work, input/output bounds, and raw edge-triggered drain/rearm responsibilities are explicit. Generic aliases are scoped to the original pattern rather than duplicate articles.

runnable_example.verification: Exact four-line demo output on real local stream sockets; all 32 fragmentations of two LF-delimited records preserve framing; multiple records per recv; empty, exactly eight-byte, and arbitrary binary payload boundaries; ninth payload byte closes only the offending reader without needing LF; incomplete A does not stall B; EOF discards only an unfinished suffix and retains completed records; clean EOF emits nothing; actual registered callbacks tolerate would-block without state loss; an instrumented real-socket adapter verifies one recv of at most four bytes per callback; OSError triggers connection error cleanup while RuntimeError remains visible; real-socket lifecycle instrumentation verifies unregister before close and selector release; independent per-connection buffers, nonblocking read interests, duplicate-registration failure, and fixture cleanup. No selector fairness, listener, write dispatcher, TLS, worker pool, durable sink, global backpressure, authentication, or production throughput claim is inferred.

example_limits: Original Python 3.11+ read-only collector using real local stream socket pairs and DefaultSelector. One loop thread owns successfully registered readers and dispatches callbacks sequentially. Each callback attempts one nonblocking recv of at most four bytes. Arbitrary-byte records use LF delimiters and 0–8 payload bytes; the ninth unfinished payload byte rejects only that connection. Per-connection fragments survive callbacks; EOF rejects an unfinished suffix without rolling back earlier complete records. Would-block returns control, OSError records connection failure and cleans up, and unexpected programming errors remain visible. Readers unregister before close and finally releases the selector. The fixture sends tiny blocking writes outside callbacks and uses a two-second progress timeout, not a production deadline. Result/error lists retain output and are not a bounded production sink. No public listener, write dispatcher, TLS, worker pool, durable sink, complete admission/backpressure policy, authentication, callback fairness, throughput guarantee, or raw edge-triggered implementation is inferred.
